title: Cuba Life Expectancy Falls for First Time in 75 Years Under Illegal US Blockade
content:
Life expectancy in Cuba has fallen for the first time since 1950 as the island nation’s healthcare system buckles under a US-imposed economic and fuel blockade.




World Health Organisation (WHO) head Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus 

called for the blockade to be lifted

 on Tuesday and warned US sanctions are endangering the lives of Cuban children.




Tedros said life expectancy in Cuba had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025 – the first decline since records began in 1950.




US president Donald Trump began escalating a decades-long economic embargo on Cuba during his first term, and this year sparked an acute humanitarian crisis by imposing a fuel blockade. 




This has led to medics struggling with daily power outages amid critical shortages of food, medicines and specialised baby formula. 




Cuban officials say 

only a single tanker of oil 

has reached the island since January, crippling the country’s electrical grid. 




On a three-day visit to Havana, Tedros outlined how Cuba’s infant mortality rate more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, and maternal mortality increased from 37.4 per 1,000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 last year.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: US Military Set to Detonate Toxic Lead Bomb in Iowa
content:
Children, pregnant women and chronically ill people in Iowa are being advised to evacuate as the US army prepares to blow up a stockpile of munitions laced with lead on Wednesday. 




Nearly five tonnes of unstable bomb-making chemicals stored at a base in Middletown, Iowa, are scheduled for detonation despite serious risks to human health. 




The detonation is expected to send a toxic plume of lead-containing dust particles over eastern Iowa and into the neighbouring state of Illinois, where toxins will likely settle on farmland, homes and playgrounds. 




There is no safe level of exposure to lead, which is a neurotoxin. 




350 farms could be exposed

 to the toxic lead dust, according to the US Department of Agriculture. 




Children and pregnant women are particularly at risk as exposure to lead can interfere with fetal brain development, cause cognitive damage and increase the likelihood of miscarriages and premature births. 




In adults, lead exposure is linked to decreased kidney function, fertility issues and heart problems, along with

 increased risks

 of various cancers.




Iowa has the 

second-highest rate of cancer

 among US states, and is one of only three states where rates of cancer are rising. 




A lawsuit was filed by environmental groups to block the detonation, but the US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Monday that it could go ahead.

author: Ana Naomi De Sousa
title: ‘No Dignified Way to Live’: Why Portugal Is Rising up Over Housing
content:
Edmilson Tavares Fonseca didn’t join the thousands of people who marched through Lisbon last Saturday to protest against Portugal’s rising living costs and unaffordable housing. Saturday is the only day he gets to spend with his partner and their baby. The rest of the week, he works two jobs, trying to make ends meet. Still, he identifies strongly with the protesters. “The people in the streets right now are demanding what most people in Portugal want,” he says. “The government have shut their eyes to reality – but we don’t have a dignified way to live right now.” 




Fonseca grew up in the Lisbon suburb of Cova da Moura, known for its precarious self-built housing. He still works full-time in the area, supporting marginalised young people, but goes home to a different part of the city, where he lives in a rented apartment with his partner. They can afford it, for now, but since becoming parents, and with average rents in the city having almost doubled since 2017, Fonseca and his partner long for the security of owning their own home. Fonseca took a second job as an Uber driver to supplement his income, but, despite this, he has been refused a mortgage four times. “Sometimes it feels as if all the sacrifices I’m making are for nothing,” he says, “it’s so demoralising”.




Fonseca’s story shows what Portugal’s housing crisis means for ordinary people. Since 2015, house prices 

have outstripped wage growth by 60%

 – by far the widest gap in the EU, where the average is 6.8%. Meanwhile, public housing makes up less than 2% of the country’s housing stock.




Last weekend’s protest marked five weeks of people in Portugal taking to the streets over the housing crisis. Spontaneous 

encampments have sprung up from Porto to Lisbon

, and tens of thousands have turned out to weekly demonstrations, 

defying violence

 and disparagement from the authorities. As the gaping discrepancy between house prices and wages pushes both renting and buying far beyond what most can afford, people in Portugal are starting to question where all the money has gone – and who really owns the cities they live in.




“What we’re seeing now is the failure of public policies to respond to national housing needs over several decades, resulting in a deep-rooted crisis,” says Ana Cordeiro Santos, an economist at Coimbra University. 




After property prices crashed during the 2011 debt crisis, the government responded to a shortage of capital and widespread urban decay by courting foreign investment in real estate, Cordeiro Santos says. A central pillar of this strategy was the Golden Visa scheme, which offered residency – and eventually a route to citizenship to non-EU nationals who invested at least €500,000 (£420,000) in property.

 Between 2012 and 2023, it brought in €6.5bn in property investment, with most visas going to Chinese (43%), Brazilian (10%) and United States (6%) nationals, fuelling further speculation in real estate.




The flood of global capital has generated huge profits for investors, but

 made the housing market 

completely unaffordable

 for ordinary Portuguese people. In Lisbon, the average net salary is currently €1,405 (£1,190) a month – while the average one-bedroom flat rents for around €1,450 (£1,230).




Frederico Ascensão da Natividade Prazeres, a 24-year-old software engineer, says he “made all the sensible choices” – and now feels “deeply betrayed”. Despite earning €2,200 (£1,860) a month, a high salary in Portugal, especially for his age, he can’t afford to live alone in the Lisbon neighbourhood where he grew up. Instead, he rents a room in a shared three-bedroom apartment with no living room, splitting his time between his bedroom and the kitchen. “I live like a rat,” he says.




He checks property websites every couple of weeks, but would have to move at least 80km away to buy. Now he’s thinking of going further – to Switzerland. Portugal’s Emigration Observatory estimates that around 65,000 people left the country in 2024. “There is an urban exodus of people of my generation,” Prazeres says. “We really don’t want to leave, but we feel we have no choice.”




So many young people are leaving Portugal just as it has become one of Europe’s most desirable destinations. Tourist overnight stays have more than doubled since 2012, helped by the deregulation of the rental market, tax breaks for short-term lets on platforms such as Airbnb, and budget airlines like easyJet and Ryanair. “Tourism has boosted the economy, but it has had an adverse impact on housing,” says Cordeiro Santos. “It takes up land and property that could meet people’s needs, reducing supply and pushing up prices.”




More recently, the government has courted “digital nomads”: remote workers earning at least €3,680 (£3,110) a month – four times the Portuguese minimum wage – with more than €11,000 (£9,300) in savings. They receive residency, a route to citizenship and, until 2024, access to generous tax breaks

. More than 22% currently come from the US, followed by 8% from the UK – the number of British immigrants to Portugal has 

tripled in the last decade

. With their incomes, they can outbid most locals for housing.




As discontent has grown, successive governments have made modest changes. In 2023, the then Socialist government suspended new licences for short-term lets in much of the country and removed property investment from the Golden Visa scheme; a tax regime that offered foreign residents years of low or zero tax on overseas income was also closed to newcomers in 2024. But none of these measures have brought rents or house prices within reach of local wages. Meanwhile, 

 Portugal’s current housing deficit is 

estimated at around 300,000 homes.




“The fact that house prices are still rising shows government measures to date have not worked,” says Cordeiro Santos. She points to a mix of ideology and vested interests: “Portugal’s government – which is already ideologically opposed to regulation – is now extremely dependent on real estate for economic growth, and that makes it even harder for it to act against the sector’s interests.”




“We have low salaries, job precariousness, and scant state support, but interest rates just keep going up,” says Cordeiro Santos. “Portuguese people feel their living conditions declining and their purchasing power decreasing. There are a lot of consequences – for example, the state cannot attract the professionals it needs, and [we] have a shortage of doctors, nurses, and teachers.”




It is ripple effects like these that have been behind 

the huge national demonstrations

 since October, with housing protests in 32 Portuguese cities in one weekend in November alone.




Conservative prime minister Luís Montenegro has refused calls to engage with protesters directly – despite the Casa Para Viver [Home to Live] platform, which represents over 100 national housing movements, making repeated public requests for a meeting. 




Earlier this year, Montenegro’s government 

pushed through legislation that favours landlords’ rights

, abolishing rent caps and making it easier to carry out evictions. Montenegro – whose 2025 campaign slogan was ‘L

et Luís get on with his job

‘ – had previously pledged to construct 133,000 new homes for low-income families by 2030, but recently told journalists “you can’t build houses overnight”. 




While Montenegro and his government say they need more time, Fonseca is among those debating giving up on a future in Portugal: his partner wants to emigrate. “We can’t have any more children in these conditions, which is something we both want,” he says. “She’s had enough of the situation here – if it was up to her we’d be gone already.”

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Amnesty: Investigate Israel for Genocidal Act of Preventing Births in Gaza
content:
Israel should be investigated for the genocidal act of preventing births in Gaza, Amnesty International has said in a new report.




The 

135-page report

, released on Wednesday, documents a “pattern of wide-scale reproductive harm”, including Israeli attacks on maternity hospitals, the displacement of and attacks on pregnant women, attacks on IVF facilities and the destruction of embryos, alongside Israel’s blockade on food and medical supplies. 




Israel has continued to perpetrate gendered violence against women and girls in Gaza despite the so-called ceasefire of October 2025. 




The report presents evidence that Israel has imposed measures that ultimately prevent births in Gaza, and calls for Israel to be investigated for the crime of genocide by imposing measures intended to prevent births, which is prohibited under Article II (d) of the Genocide Convention. 




It highlights how pregnant women miscarried due to Israeli attacks, gave birth prematurely due to malnutrition, and were forced to give birth under fire. Attacks on Gaza’s reproductive healthcare services include the destruction of around 5,000 embryos in a strike on the occupied territory’s largest IVF clinic. 




Through hundreds of interviews – including over 120 with women and girls in Gaza – and analysis of photographs, videos and medical records, the report documents the specifically gendered dimensions of Israel’s genocide.




It finds that Israel has deliberately denied women and girls in Gaza access to essential healthcare through the systematic destruction of medical and reproductive services, forcibly displaced them into degrading and unsanitary conditions and starved them over the past three years.




A woman identified as Sara told Amnesty: “Right after I gave birth, they placed me in a room to rest. About an hour later, snipers fired directly at the room. I remember five bullets hitting the room. It was a miracle that neither my baby nor I was hit. I had to remain in the hospital under total siege for 18 days. Snipers were positioned all around it, shooting at anyone who moved. I saw a cleaner shot and killed in front of me.” 




A doctor at Al-Kheir maternity hospital in Khan Younis described attacks, a raid and forced evacuations by Israeli forces in January 2024, where women “who had just delivered, especially with a caesarean section, had to flee while still heavily bleeding and their catheter still connected, carrying their newborn babies”.




A healthcare professional in north Gaza said their hospital had seen an increase in premature births, and they “had to watch these premature babies die, without the ability to provide the intensive care, medicines, nutrients and antibiotics they urgently need”. 




The bodies of babies were found decomposing in incubators in a Gaza City hospital’s pediatric ICU 

in December 2023 

after the Israeli military forced staff and patients to evacuate during its ground invasion. 




Israel’s blockade on aid entering Gaza has created severe shortages of baby formula, with Israeli authorities 

even confiscating individual cans

 of infant formula packed by doctors entering the territory.  




The report finds that Palestinian women and girls have been killed at an “unprecedented” and “exceptional” scale due to Israeli forces systematically targeting homes and makeshift shelters – some of which killed entire multi-generational families – and using heavy explosive weapons on densely populated civilian areas.




Amnesty finds that at least 85 women and girls from Gaza were held in Israeli detention between 7 October 2023 and early 2026, and of the 12 interviewed, none had been charged with any crime. They reported being subjected to beatings, sexual violence, strip searches and rape threats, being denied underwear, and seeing male soldiers urinating on Palestinian girls in Israeli detention. 




A 15-year-old girl described women waiting in long lines to request sanitary towels while male soldiers mocked them and laughed at their blood-stained clothing.




Interviewees also shared humiliating experiences of displacement, and the pain and trauma of losing their homes. One interviewee, Najia, said the only toilet facility she could access had no roof and was shared by 13 families. She said she was “carrying out a slow suicide, refusing to drink so I would not have to stand exposed beneath a hail of bombs and glares, until it felt like my kidneys would burst”. 




Amnesty International UK is calling on the UK government to fulfil its obligations to prevent and punish genocide and use “all available means to pressure Israel to stop blocking humanitarian access, particularly medical equipment and reconstruction materials needed for healthcare facilities”. 




Amnesty’s report also finds Israel is continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in Gaza in two other ways. Firstly, by inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about physical destruction and, secondly, by causing serious bodily`and mental harm to members of the group. 




Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza, including over 13,000 adult women and 9,000 girls. Tens of thousands more women have suffered life-changing injuries, and are carrying profound trauma and grief from the killing or disappearances of their loved ones.

author: Steven Methven
title: AI Has Come for the Maths Nerds
content:
A bit of an odd one today (and an even one too) as I take the unexpected step of writing about numbers. But unexpected was the name of the game this weekend after a mathematician at AI giant Anthropic announced that he’d used Claude to solve 

one of maths’ most famous problems

.




The form of the AI-generated proof and the fact that it may take humans many years to understand it sure looks like magic. But is it wizardry or sleight of hand? And does it prove what we’ve all anxiously been thinking: the machines are getting too smart for our own good? 

Don’t worry, you won’t be asked to show your working.




Maths is often described as the science of patterns. So when mathematicians find objects that don’t seem to follow one, they get very excited. That’s why the prime numbers get them buzzing.




A prime number is any number larger than 1 and divisible only by 1 and itself. At the beginning of the number line, they come at you fast: 2, 3, 5, 7. By the time you count to ten, 40% of those numbers are prime. As you go on, they thin out. Once you reach 100, only a quarter of the numbers you’ve passed are prime. And if you’ve counted them that far, you’ll have noticed they don’t appear in a regular pattern. Often, they come in pairs, separated by just one number – like 11 and 13. But sometimes they’ll pop up alone, like, poor old 89, the loneliest of all. 




You can never predict exactly where a prime will turn up. But using a separate piece of maths, you can say 

approximately

 how many primes there are in a given stretch of numbers. That approximation is usually slightly wrong. But since we can’t check all the numbers (like Lime Bikes, there are just too many), we don’t know that there won’t be stretches where it’s 

very 

wrong – great prime-free deserts or spans where they crowd like pigeons on a chip. 




The 167-year old Riemann hypothesis says that can’t happen. Its super-complicated maths sets a limit on how wrong we can be. If it’s true, it means the primes behave in an orderly fashion. It now turns out 

it’s very probably true

. Finally, mathematicians can unclench.  




But it’s the rest of us clenching, instead. 




Last Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge posted 

a statement on his website

 claiming that, using an unreleased version of Claude, he proved the hypothesis in around six weeks. He described how, while he’d begun by steering Claude, the AI “far outpaced me near the finish line”. Alpöge gets even more gushy. “Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled,” he wrote, “Claude began to leave me in awe.”




The timing of that almost advertorial language raised suspicions, with Alpöge’s history-making announcement coming just a day after 

Anthropic’s stock market launch

. The intervening 24 hours saw Anthropic stock 

fall by a little under 10%

. For his part, Alpöge has said it was his decision to publish the proof, rather than that of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. 




I say ‘publish the proof’. It isn’t published, not in any way the rest of us can read. Instead, it’s been compiled in over 17m lines of Lean code – a widely-used piece of proof-checking software. By Saturday, after several computer checks, it was 

declared valid

.  



















The Cortado

 





          Get your shot of political analysis from 

Ash Sarkar

 and 

Steven Methven

, every Monday and Friday morning.

Nor will it be readable by humans anytime soon. In his note, Alpöge claimed compiling it in English had reached more than 250k pages. Naturally, that leaves questions about what’s in it, and its value as a proof. Knowing that the hypothesis is true will please a lot of mathematicians, who’ve anyway been treating it as true for ages. But for many, 

the test will be more demanding

. Does the proof discover new areas of maths? Does it invent novel techniques? And does it come with insight into 

why

 the hypothesis is true? It’s via proofs with those qualities that human maths has often progressed. 




Perhaps, though, the days of human maths are over. If so, maths as a profession is in trouble. Could those who once slowly carved out great palaces of human knowledge now become mere scribes, puzzling out the speedy gospel of machines? 




And what about us, the non-nerds struggling to understand all this? Well, the proof has zero immediate impact. But its existence should give real pause. If Alpöge’s description of events is true, then a motivated AI has done in six weeks what our most brilliant humans couldn’t in well over 150 years. It’s hard not to call that intelligent. Which means now may be the time to 

hit the brakes

.

content:
Everyone agrees the West is in decline. But who’s really to blame? Owen Jones has the answers in his new book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It. In conversation with Ash Sarkar, with a live audience at EartH Hackney, Jones traces a line from the collapse of the Soviet Union through to the atrocity of the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians, and Donald Trump’s military defeat by Iran.

So what is actually happening there and who can you trust?

He talks to Richard Hames about Uyghur life before the crackdown, the surveillance system that spans from tracking software on phones to continuous checkpoints to security service agents living in Uyghurs’ houses. He describes the camps and system of forced labour, and why he calls the whole system “terror capitalism”, a frontier where settler colonialism merges with the tech industry.

title: Andy Burnham’s Government Is (Still) Coming for Jury Trials
content:
Palestine and climate protesters who are accused of breaking the law face being tried by magistrates instead of a jury of their peers, according to government plans to speed up the justice system.




Legal experts say the plans to slash access to jury trials will have profound consequences for protest cases, racialised minorities, public participation in the justice system and our fundamental rights.




The Starmer-era Courts and Tribunals Bill will remove defendants’ right to request a jury trial for offences of medium seriousness – known as “either-way” or “each-way” offences. It will also expand magistrates’ powers, reduce rights to appeal and earmark some offences for judge-only trials. 




The bill was introduced in February by then-justice secretary David Lammy as an attempt to deal with severe court backlogs in England and Wales and help victims get justice faster. The backlogs in criminal courts are real, but the bill goes significantly beyond 

Lord Leveson’s  recommendations

 for dealing with the issue. 




And while Andy Burnham’s government claims it has 

“changed course”

 by scrapping one part of the bill, in practice the legislation will still cut access to trial by jury. 




How will the Courts and Tribunals Bill affect jury trials?




All criminal cases in England and Wales start at magistrates’ court. Currently, defendants charged with an either-way offence – such as theft, burglary, drug violations and criminal damage where the value exceeds £5k – can elect for a jury trial at Crown Court. The Courts and Tribunals Bill will remove this right, leaving it up to magistrates to decide whether a case remains in their court for a summary trial where there is no jury, or is sent to Crown Court. 




Magistrates will be empowered to impose longer prison sentences for single either-way offences, increasing the current maximum sentence a magistrate can give from 12 months to two years. 




Moreover, defendants’ automatic right to appeal their conviction or sentence from a magistrates’ court to Crown Court will be removed – instead, they’ll have to ask permission from the Crown Court to appeal. 




The government has scrapped a controversial clause in the bill that would mean offences likely to result in a prison sentence of up to three years were only heard by judges, after justice secretary Alex Norris said he had “heard the strength of feeling on the proposals for increasing the number of judge-alone trials in the Crown Court”.




However, other clauses restricting jury trials remain, meaning that far fewer defendants will be tried by a jury of their peers – a fundamental right and 

inheritance from the 1215 Magna Carta

. 




Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director 

Tom Southerden described this as Burnham’s administration “astutely judging a concession they can afford to make and get political credit for”, while retaining measures that “add up to very 

significant ongoing threats to jury trial in this country”. 




Tim Crosland, a former government lawyer, previous head of legal for the National Criminal Intelligence Service and co-founder of campaign group Defend Our Juries, agreed, telling Novara Media that Burnham’s government is claiming to be supportive of jury trials while “continuing to undermine them by stealth”. 




“Removing a defendant’s right to trial by jury in either-way cases is a profound constitutional change, which the government is trying to force through without any political mandate, and with minimal parliamentary scrutiny,” Crosland said. 




“Tackling the backlog in the criminal justice system doesn’t explain it. Shifting cases to the magistrates’ court only increases the backlog in the magistrates’ court. It’s robbing Peter to pay Paul.”




Southernden told Novara Media that the “watering down” of appeal rights from magistrates’ courts is “a real problem”, and highlighted 

how the bill risks

 making trials less fair for racialised defendants.   




“Juries have been functioning as quite a significant safety valve for systemic racism in the justice system,” Southernden said. “Members of racialised minorities statistically choose jury trials over magistrates’ trials at 

a much higher rate

 than white people do, because juries are a more reliable source of racially neutral decision-making 

than magistrates are

 for the same offences.




“Juries are one of the few things in the justice system that are found to be not systemically racist in their outcomes.”




Which cases will receive judge-only trials?




Another controversial part of the bill concerns “complex or lengthy” Crown Court cases, which will, if the bill passes in its current form, be dealt with by judge-only trials. 




While complex or lengthy cases are largely presented as fraud and economic crime-related offences, the bill has been 

criticised for failing to include

 any clear definition of – or limitation on – the offences that could be denied a jury trial.




Southernden also warned against the idea that some cases can only be understood by “elites”. “I think it’s important that we reject the notion that juries are incapable of understanding these things,” he said. “If they are, it’s a failing in the law and the way the law is presented.” 




The bill will also allow the secretary of state to add offences to the list of those eligible for a judge-only trial via secondary legislation. There is currently no restriction on the type of offences that can be added. 




A

 House of 

Lords 

committee has slammed

 this proposal as an “inappropriate delegation of power” and a controversial use of “Henry VIII powers” – which enable ministers to amend or repeal legislation with little parliamentary scrutiny.




“The prospect of the secretary of state picking and choosing categories of cases to hand over [to judges only] is hugely problematic,” Southernden added.




The bill has met strong opposition from industry professionals, with the

 Criminal Bar Association

 saying it is “fundamentally opposed to the proposed restrictions on the right to jury trial”. Its own survey of criminal barristers showed around 90% were against the proposals.




These plans were entirely absent from Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, giving weight to the impression that the parts of the bill that limit jury trials target political protest cases. 




How will the Courts and Tribunals Bill impact protest cases?




Crosland believes this is a bill designed to prevent political cases, such as those concerning protest-related offences, going in front of juries. 




“The real driver for these plans is the government’s determination to stop juries reaching the wrong verdicts in political trials,” he said. “It’s deeply embarrassing for powerful people when juries side with those exposing their crimes, whether that’s complicity in climate breakdown or aiding and abetting a genocide. 




“Jury conscience has become a powerful site of democratic resistance to the abuse of power. But if we want to hold on to it, now is the time to organise in defence of it.”




The bill is making its way through parliament at a time when hundreds of peaceful protesters have been 

charged under the Terrorism Act 

for demonstrating against the government’s ban on Palestine Action, and more cases related to anti-genocide direct action are still pending following the sentencing of four activists 

as terrorists after being found guilty of criminal damage

 against arms manufacturer Elbit Systems.




Southernden pointed to how in protest cases “judges are increasingly excluding defences from them and excluding evidence from trials” – 

a key issue in the trial 

of the four Palestine Action activists earlier this year.




“Defendants increasingly err on the side of trying to communicate with a jury about the justice of what they’re being put through,” he said, “and that will be removed from them by the current proposals.” 




The bill has already passed through the House of Commons, and members of the House of Lords began their detailed examination of the legislation on 10 November.

title: Is France Prosecuting a Palestinian Refugee on Evidence Extracted by Israeli Torture?
content:
How might a hostile state pursue a refugee beyond its borders? This is a question some fear is at the heart of a case currently inching its way through 

France’s special-track antiterrorist justice system

. 




Four UN special rapporteurs have warned that 2024 charges brought against “Ali O”, a Palestinian national who held refugee status in France, are built on compromised evidence provided by Israel. 




“We are concerned that Ali’s arrest, detention and prosecution appear to be based on information obtained through the use of torture and other forms of abuse against Palestinians by Israeli authorities,” wrote the UN experts, including human rights lawyer Francesca Albanese, in a 28 August communication issued to France and 

published in late October

.




After fleeing Palestine, Ali O settled in France in 2016 and obtained formal recognition as a refugee in 2020. Married to a French citizen and the father of French children, he was arrested at his home in Strasbourg in May 2024. He was subsequently indicted for charges of terrorist financing and conspiracy connected to militant activity in the occupied West Bank in early 2023. 




A memo from the French intelligence services to the country’s refugee administration, and included in the litigation file seen by Novara Media, claims the defendant “participated in the transfer of funds and weapons with military aims” to Palestinian armed groups.




The investigation against Ali O was opened in late 2023. Though French criminal procedure precludes the defence from uncovering certain state evidence, the French state alleges that the defendant was a past member of the Fatah Hawks, a militant group linked to the al-Aqsa Martyrs’ Brigades and affiliated with the Fatah faction of the Palestine Liberation Organisation. It also claims that the defendant conducted online searches on websites used for the dissemination of guerilla tactics and weaponry. 




“[Ali O] committed several crimes incompatible with refugee status. Our service proposes withdrawing refugee status for the concerned party,” wrote the French intelligence bureau. Authorities revoked Ali O’s refugee status in February 2025, even though he has yet to be convicted and is therefore presumed to be innocent.   




Dismissing these accusations, Ali O’s counsel claimed allegations like these would be difficult to construct without close collaboration with outside state sources, notably Israeli. “Ali’s dossier demonstrates the degree to which the French justice system has accepted the role of a subcontractor for Israeli authorities,” attorney Raphaël Kempf told Novara Media, placing his client’s case in the wider crackdown and surveillance of Palestinian nationals residing in Europe. 




Irregularities in the case file also point to Israeli influence in the case against Ali O. The French intelligence memo stipulates he participated from France in militant activity in “Judea and Samaria,” i.e. the Israeli state’s official designation for the West Bank, which is internationally recognised as Palestinian territory, including by France. 




France’s anti-terrorism prosecutorial service (PNAT) declined

 Novara Media’s request for comment. 




Ali O isn’t an unknown quantity for the Israeli state. 




Born in 1990 and raised in the Balata refugee camp on the outskirts of the West Bank city of Nablus, Ali O was 14 years old when he witnessed his younger brother’s killing by an Israeli soldier. Two years later, he was arrested and held in extrajudicial detention before receiving a four-year prison sentence for throwing stones at Israeli occupation forces. It was the first of many stints in jail, according to the biographical information compiled by activists with the Free Ali committee. After his last release from Israeli detention in 2014, he fled to Europe, passing through Italy and Switzerland before making it to France. 




“France recognised [Ali O] as a refugee because of his well-founded fear of persecution by Israeli authorities,” UN special rapporteur on torture Pau Pérez-Sales said at a 29 October press conference following the publication of the co-signed notice to the French government. 




The case against Ali O is based on evidence gathered by Israel from three Palestinian sources. The UN memo warns that one witness, Ali O’s brother, was tortured on several occasions and there are grounds to presume that the other two sources were tortured as well, habitual practices for Palestinians held in Israeli captivity. None of the three were represented by an attorney. 




While the French government is within its right to investigate criminal activities, including cases related to terrorism, “France has an obligation to ensure that its judicial system does not rely on declarations and evidence obtained under torture,” said Pérez-Sales.




Kempf accused the French government of double standards. “The justice system is making the choice to pursue Ali for these charges, just as it is making the choice to not investigate allegations made by my client over the use of torture in the evidence now being used against him,” he said. “By accepting to be the relay for Israel’s accusations against my client, France is de facto validating these types of practices.”




For Kempf, a deeper question remains France’s recourse to terrorism charges in Ali O’s case, pointing to the UN’s recusal of the qualification of terrorism for Palestinian militant activity taking place within an ongoing colonial conflict and occupation. “French prosecutors are operating in a vacuum and are pretending that the outside world just does not exist,” he said. 




A hearing on Ali O’s ongoing pre-trial detention is scheduled for 23 November.

content:

The attack on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza took place in the early hours of Thursday, local media and Gaza’s health ministry reported.




The doctor killed has been named Dr Rizq Abu Shaeira, and described by Al Jazeera as “a significant and prominent surgeon”.

title: Millions of Workers Shut Down Spain With First General Strike in 14 Years
content:
Spanish workers braved stormy weather to go on general strike in protest against the country’s housing crisis on Wednesday.




Unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers, as millions downed tools three weeks before a snap general election. There were 

“total stoppages”

Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector are also taking part, they added. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% are striking while 35% of postal service workers have also joined.




The 24-hour strike, Spain’s first in 14 years, is backed by the country’s two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants’ associations fighting rising rents and evictions.




“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.




Mass protest marches were planned for Wednesday afternoon despite the expected arrival of two storms, Charles and Bruna.




Unions pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand across the country, saying it shows that activity in energy-intensive industries such as steel processing had come to a halt.

content:

Representatives from more than 100 ports will participate in the international day of action on 30 October, calling for an end to Israel’s genocide against Palestinians and “US-Israeli wars of aggression”.

title: Met Police Lawyers Told Officer Her PTSD Was Not Severe Because She Was Only Raped Once
content:

DC Linda Williams sued her employer in 2022 for failing to protect her against serial rapist PC David Carrick, who attacked her while they were working together in south London in 2004. 




But Williams, 60, who waived her right to anonymity to 

share her story with the BBC

The lawyers were officially representing Met police commissioner Mark Rowley, so Williams – who is still a serving officer – is calling for his resignation. 




“As far as I am concerned, it is Mark Rowley, the commissioner, saying these terrible things, as he was the defendant in the case,” she said. Rowley has failed in his promise to fix a toxic culture within the force, she added. 




The start of her civil case against the Met was “when the suicidal thoughts really came in,” she said, adding that force did not “believe anything” she said and that its behaviour felt “like being raped all over again”.

title: Over 20k Sign Petition Demanding Inquiry Into UK Role in Gaza Genocide
content:
